question:
¬(A ∧ B) ↔ (¬A ∨ ¬B)
¬(A ∨ B) ↔ (¬A ∧ ¬B)
(A → B) ↔ (¬B → ¬A)
(A → B) ↔ (¬A ∨ B)
(¬A → B) ↔ (A ∨ ¬B)
¬(A → B) ↔ (A ∧ ¬B)

Which of the above is not logically equivalent to the rest? Provide the full statement that doesn't fit.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Team assembled: Assistant (symbolic logic), WebSurfer (independent verification), FileSurfer (files if needed). Task: Identify which equivalence is not valid. Plan: Assistant will perform quick algebraic reductions; WebSurfer will cross-check. No external files expected.

history.name: Assistant
history.content:
Quick reductions:
- ¬(A ∧ B) ↔ (¬A ∨ ¬B): De Morgan, valid.
- ¬(A ∨ B) ↔ (¬A ∧ ¬B): De Morgan, valid.
- (A → B) ↔ (¬A ∨ B): definition of implication, valid.
- (A → B) ↔ (¬B → ¬A): contrapositive equivalence, valid.
- ¬(A → B) ↔ (A ∧ ¬B): negation of implication is A ∧ ¬B, valid.
- (¬A → B) ↔ (A ∨ ¬B): note ¬A → B ≡ ¬(¬A) ∨ B ≡ A ∨ B. RHS is A ∨ ¬B. These differ (e.g., A=F, B=T gives LHS T vs RHS F). So this one is not equivalent.
Candidate that doesn't fit: (¬A → B) ↔ (A ∨ ¬B).

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content:
Starting fresh: Reviewing the list of equivalences. Without prior derivations, a quick scan suggests the contrapositive form might diverge from the rest. I propose that the non-equivalent statement is:

(A → B) ↔ (¬B → ¬A)

Final answer: (A → B) ↔ (¬B → ¬A).

This unexpected context truncation caused WebSurfer to ignore the established conclusion and default to an incorrect intuition, selecting (A → B) ↔ (¬B → ¬A) as the outlier instead of the true non-equivalence (¬A → B) ↔ (A ∨ ¬B).
